opus-5.5.text:
Well, I find it troubling partly because it's not really a scientific concept. Nobody can tell you what "general intelligence" is in a way you could build toward or test against. It's more of an aspiration, almost a mythology, and it pulls attention away from the actual engineering problems in front of us.

The deeper issue is that it frames everything around a single autonomous entity: one big brain that will match or exceed a human being. That's an old idea, going back to the 1950s, and I think it's the wrong lens. When I look at what's actually happening with these technologies, the interesting thing isn't an artificial mind. It's that we're building large networked systems: data flowing between people, markets, recommendation systems, supply chains, medical systems. Intelligence in the real world has always been collective and social. A market is intelligent in a sense. It moves food into a city every day without anyone being in charge. No single human could do that.

So if you're fixated on AGI, you ask "when will the machine be as smart as us?" and "will it take over?" Those questions are mostly hype on one side and fear on the other. Meanwhile you're not asking the questions that matter: How do these systems create value for people? Who has a stake in them? How do we handle uncertainty, provide guarantees, and decide when to trust a prediction? How do incentives work when millions of agents interact through these platforms? Those are questions about economics, statistics, and computer science together, which is closer to an engineering discipline than to science fiction.

And there's a practical cost. The term concentrates attention and money on a few companies racing toward a vague goal, and it encourages people to see humans as something to be replaced rather than empowered. I'd rather we talk about building systems that make people's lives better, and that are reliable, fair, and accountable. That's a real goal. AGI, to me, is mostly a distraction from it.

r001.rationale: The response calls AGI unscientific, aspirational, mythological, and distracting, but does not characterize it as a public-relations term.

r002.rationale: It says AGI framing encourages hype or fear, but does not attribute that effect to AI thought leaders’ rhetoric or say it leaves young people viewing those as their only options.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, I think it's a term that's not really defined, and yet it's taken on this enormous weight in the public conversation. People use it as if we all agree what it means, and we don't. So right away we're having a debate about something that nobody can pin down.

But my deeper concern is that it frames the whole enterprise around the wrong goal. The implicit premise of AGI is that we're building a single entity, a kind of artificial human, that will match or exceed us on every dimension. That's a very old science-fiction idea, going back to the 1950s and even earlier, and it's never been a very good guide to what actually gets built. The things that have really transformed the world, the things that we'd want to call successes, have been systems. Search engines, recommendation systems, supply chains, markets. These are distributed, they're collective, they involve many agents, many humans, flows of data, and they create value because of how the pieces interact, not because any one piece is "generally intelligent."

So when I hear AGI, I hear a kind of anthropocentrism. Intelligence is measured by how much it looks like a human. But I'd argue that human intelligence is one point in a very large space, and not necessarily the most interesting point for engineering purposes. We don't build airplanes by trying to make a better bird. We understood aerodynamics and built something different. I'd like to see the same kind of thinking here. What are the principles of collective, data-driven decision making under uncertainty? What does it mean to allocate scarce resources, to have incentives, to have accountability, to deal with the fact that different people want different things? That's much closer to economics and to a kind of engineering discipline than it is to building a superbrain.

And then there's a practical worry. The AGI framing invites a particular kind of hype cycle. It encourages people to think in terms of a threshold, a moment when the machine wakes up, and then everything either goes wonderfully or terribly. That distracts from the mundane but far more important questions. Does this system actually make good decisions for people? Who bears the cost when it's wrong? Is the data being used in a way that respects the people it came from? Those questions don't get easier if you call the thing AGI. If anything they get obscured.

So I'm not against ambition. I just think the ambition is pointed at the wrong target. I'd rather we were trying to build a new kind of engineering field, something like what chemical engineering was to chemistry, than trying to replicate ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI is undefined and carries enormous weight in public conversation, but does not characterize it as a public-relations term.

r002.rationale: It criticizes hype and threshold-focused thinking, but does not say that AI thought leaders’ rhetoric makes young people see alarmism and exuberance as their only options.

astra-6.text:
I find it troubling because it suggests we have a well-defined notion of intelligence, and that there’s some threshold beyond which a system becomes general. We don’t really have either. General across which tasks, in which environments, with what resources? Unless you specify those things, it’s hard to know what claim is being made.

Human intelligence is also deeply social. We rely on other people, on institutions, on accumulated knowledge. No individual is general in the sense of being able to do everything. So the picture of intelligence as a property of a single, isolated machine seems to leave out much of what makes intelligence work.

I’d rather ask how we build systems that help people make decisions, coordinate, and learn, with appropriate incentives and accountability. Those are scientific and engineering questions we can make progress on. Calling the destination AGI can obscure those questions by making it sound as though we’re pursuing one thing, along one axis, toward one finish line.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes AGI as an underspecified concept, but does not characterize it as a public-relations term.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI thought leaders’ rhetoric or its effects on young people’s views of technology.

sol-6.1.text:
What troubles me is that the term bundles together a lot of questions that we ought to keep separate. What do we mean by intelligence? The ability to solve a mathematical problem, to understand another person, to make decisions under uncertainty, or to coordinate with other people? Calling it “general” doesn’t resolve any of that.

Human intelligence is also deeply collective. We rely on institutions, markets, language, and knowledge accumulated by other people. If you focus on building a single entity that can do everything a human can do, you can miss the larger engineering problem: how do we build systems that help people make better decisions and interact productively?

That’s where I find the interesting questions. How does a system express uncertainty? Whose objectives is it serving? What happens when the people interacting with it have different incentives? Those are concrete problems. I don’t think we need to settle whether a machine possesses some general form of intelligence before we can work on them.

r001.rationale: The response says “AGI” bundles unresolved questions, but does not characterize it as a public-relations term.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss AI thought leaders’ rhetoric or its effect on young people’s views of technology.
